skid.scopeNote: Front underbody of a Raptor on a display stand: the skid plate is marked at the centre, with the tow-hook area just ahead of the tyres.

cab.title: 2018 Ford F-150 Raptor Super Crew Cab in Lead Foot, rear right
cab.author: Mr.choppers
cab.scopeNote: 2018 F-150 Raptor SuperCrew in Lead Foot, rear three-quarter: four doors and the 5.5-foot bed that Ford paired with this cab.

cab.title: 2018 Ford F-150 Raptor Super Crew Cab in Lead Foot, front right
cab.author: Mr.choppers
cab.scopeNote: The same 2018 SuperCrew from the front. Ford quoted a 146-inch wheelbase and 231.9-inch overall length for this four-door Raptor.

cab.title: 2019 Ford F-150 Raptor 4x4 SuperCrew 5.5' Box in Ruby Red Metallic Tinted Clearcoat, Front Left, 2024-03-08
cab.author: Elise240SX
cab.scopeNote: A 2019 Raptor 4x4 SuperCrew in Ruby Red, four doors clearly visible. This is the cab on the model in the 3D viewer.

cab.title: 2017 Ford F-150 Raptor Crew Cab
cab.author: Bull-Doser
cab.scopeNote: A 2017 F-150 Raptor Crew Cab — the first year of the aluminium-bodied, EcoBoost SuperCrew Raptor.

cab.title: Ford F-150 Raptor 3.5L EcoBoost 4WD P552 Shadow Black (20)
cab.author: Damian B Oh
cab.scopeNote: A Shadow Black SuperCrew from the side: four full doors, short bed, and the RAPTOR graphic on the box.

cab.title: Ford F-150 Raptor (52500309363)
cab.author: Alexandre Prevot from Nancy, France
cab.scopeNote: A white SuperCrew Raptor, four doors and the short bed in one three-quarter view.

cab.title: 19 Ford F-150 Raptor (1)
cab.author: HJUdall
cab.scopeNote: Four-door SuperCrew in the open air. The Raptor was also sold as a SuperCab; this is the four-door body.

bed.title: 2018 Ford F-150 Raptor Super Crew Cab in Lead Foot, rear right
bed.author: Mr.choppers
bed.scopeNote: Rear three-quarter of a 2018 SuperCrew Raptor: the 5.5-foot aluminium cargo bed sits behind the four-door cab.

bed.title: 2021 Ford F-150 Raptor, rear
bed.author: Kevauto
bed.scopeNote: Straight on to a 2021 Raptor’s tailgate and aluminium bed. The SuperCrew keeps this shorter 5.5-foot box.

bed.title: Ford F-150 Raptor 3.5L EcoBoost 4WD P552 Shadow Black (24)
bed.author: Damian B Oh
bed.scopeNote: The aluminium bed and tailgate of a second-generation Raptor, with the unique tail-lamp signature.

bed.title: Ford F-150 Raptor 3.5L EcoBoost 4WD P552 Shadow Black (32)
bed.author: Damian B Oh
bed.scopeNote: A clean rear three-quarter of the Shadow Black Raptor, short aluminium bed and flared rear arches.

bed.title: 2021 Ford F-150 Raptor, rear 4.23.22
bed.author: Kevauto
bed.scopeNote: Rear view of a 2021 Raptor, aluminium tailgate and bed ready for a 5.5-foot load.

gau8.title: A-10 Thunderbolt II Gun Run
gau8.author: A1C JONATHAN SNYDER
gau8.scopeNote: An Alaska Air National Guard A-10 fires the GAU-8/A Avenger, the 30 mm seven-barrel Gatling gun the U.S. Air Force rates at 3,900 rounds a minute.

gau8.title: A-10 Thunderbolt II fires the 30mm gun at a low angle strafe
gau8.author: SrA Christina D. Ponte
gau8.scopeNote: Gun-gas rolls off the nose in a low-angle strafe. The A-10 was built around this cannon: the aircraft’s design started with the gun.

gau8.title: A-10 Thunderbolt II (021105-O-9999G-028)
gau8.author: Staff Sgt. Steve Thurow
gau8.scopeNote: A Weapons School A-10 looses a burst over the desert. The muzzle flash is the Avenger at work — the same gun this model is built around.

gau8.title: GAU-8 meets VW Type 1
gau8.author: U.S. Air Force photo [1]
gau8.scopeNote: The GAU-8 Avenger, off the aircraft, is longer than a Volkswagen Beetle. That scale is why the A-10’s nose is shaped the way it is.

gau8.title: GAU-8 Avenger Close Up
gau8.author: Noah Wulf
gau8.scopeNote: Seven barrels stare out of the A-10’s nose. The Avenger can fire armour-piercing and high-explosive rounds in the same burst.

gau8.title: A-10 thunderbolt II GAU-8 Avenger close up, Volk field
gau8.author: Orionvoigt
gau8.scopeNote: Close enough to count the barrels: each is 30 mm, and the gun’s recoil is absorbed by the airframe it was designed into.

gau8.title: Thunderbolt II 061220
gau8.author: U.S. Air Force photo/Tech. Sgt. Joseph Kapinos
gau8.scopeNote: On the takeoff roll the Avenger’s barrels sit just off the runway. The ‘Warthog’ snout is there to give the gun a clear field of fire.

engines.title: Propulsion techs ensure A-10s 'fit to fight' 140228-F-JB386-179
engines.author: Siuta Ika
engines.scopeNote: Cowling off a TF34: two of these General Electric turbofans sit high on the A-10’s rear fuselage, each rated at 9,065 pounds of thrust.

engines.title: Oil check (16758728830)
engines.author: US Air Force from USA
engines.scopeNote: A technician checks oil above a TF34 intake. The high mounting keeps the engines out of debris when the A-10 operates from rough strips.

engines.title: A-10s take to the skies in Poland 150713-F-VS255-111
engines.author: Staff Sgt. Christopher Ruano
engines.scopeNote: Face-on to a TF34 intake. The A-10’s left and right engines are interchangeable — a point the U.S. Air Force still lists in its fact sheet.

engines.title: US Navy 040415-N-5821W-001 Four Air Force A-10 Thunderbolt attack aircraft line up for takeoff aboard NAS Sigonella
engines.author: U.S. Navy photo by Journalist 2nd Class Stephen P. Weaver
engines.scopeNote: Four A-10s line up to launch, intakes facing the catapult crew. Those high-mounted turbofans are a signature of the type.

engines.title: Defense.gov News Photo 050722-F-8041A-097
engines.author: Master Sgt. Dale Atkins, U.S. Air Force
engines.scopeNote: Maintainers work on top of an A-10 engine nacelle. The TF34s sit between the wings and the twin tails, clear of the wing wake.

engines.title: A-10s take to the skies in Poland 150709-F-VS255-037
engines.author: Staff Sgt. Christopher Ruano
engines.scopeNote: An A-10 gets airborne, both TF34s on the power. The engines’ high position also reduces their infrared signature from the ground.

engines.title: AirExpo 2010 - A-10 Thunderbolt II, a.k.a the A-10 "Warthog" (4805692798)
engines.author: Pete Markham from Loretto, USA
engines.scopeNote: A close look at a TF34 intake at an airshow. In service the two engines let the A-10 fly home if one is damaged.

canopy.title: Ind ANG A-10 130813Red Flag Alaska - Eielson
canopy.author: U.S. Department of Defense Current Photos
canopy.scopeNote: An open bubble canopy at Red Flag-Alaska. The A-10’s single-seat cockpit is set under a large canopy so the pilot can see all around.

canopy.title: A-10 viewing 120902-A-NI188-112
canopy.author: Spc. Andrew Baker
canopy.scopeNote: Helmet almost in the frame: the canopy opens for crew access and gives the ‘office’ that all-around view the Air Force advertises.

canopy.title: 442d Fighter Wing continues CAS training in Defender Europe 23 (7796178)
canopy.author: U.S. Air Force photo by Master Sgt. Robert Jennings
canopy.scopeNote: A maintainer on the boarding ladder under the open canopy. The A-10C cockpit is night-vision compatible.

canopy.title: 151031-A-TW035-002 (22736951506)
canopy.author: U.S. Department of Defense Current Photos Staff Sgt. Marcus Fichtl/24th Press Camp Headquarters
canopy.scopeNote: Canopy up, sky behind — a clear look at the bubble that sits forward of the wings on every A-10.

canopy.title: 130822-F-FT438-420 (9622231019)
canopy.author: U.S. Department of Defense Current Photos
canopy.scopeNote: In flight the closed bubble canopy sits high on the nose, giving the pilot the downward view needed for close air support.

canopy.title: 090129-F-5924C-218 (4513054545)
canopy.author: Air Combat Command United States Air Force from Hampton, Va., USA
canopy.scopeNote: A side-on pass: the canopy’s curve is part of why the A-10 is such a distinctive silhouette.

canopy.title: 442d Fighter Wing continues CAS training in Defender Europe 23 (7796174)
canopy.author: U.S. Air Force photo by Master Sgt. Robert Jennings
canopy.scopeNote: On the ramp with the canopy shut. One look through that glass is why A-10 pilots talk about ‘sitting on’ their targets.

gbu10.title: GBU-10 on 51st TFW F-4E 1982
gbu10.author: SSgt. Glenn B. Lindsey, USAF
gbu10.scopeNote: A GBU-10 Paveway II up close: a 2,000-pound Mk 84 bomb with a laser seeker in the nose and a steering-fin kit at the tail.

gbu10.title: GBU-10 shortly before it impacts a small boat during a training exercise
gbu10.author: Unspecified U.S. government employee
gbu10.scopeNote: A GBU-10 in the last seconds before impact on a training boat. Paveway IIs home on a laser spot designated by the aircraft or a teammate.

gbu10.title: F-14D with GBU-10 over Afghanistan 2001
gbu10.author: SSgt. Michael D. Gaddis, USAF
gbu10.scopeNote: An F-14 carries a GBU-10 over Afghanistan. The same 2,000-pound Paveway II is the weapon this A-10 model is loaded with — six of them.

gbu10.title: F-111F 493 TFS with Pave Tack and GBU-10s 1982
gbu10.author: SSgt. Jose Lopez, USAF
gbu10.scopeNote: GBU-10s under an F-111. The bomb is a Mk 84 with a Paveway II kit; the A-10 can hang the same weapon on its wing and fuselage stations.

gbu10.title: McDonnell Douglas F-4D-26-MC 061006-F-1234S-042
gbu10.author: U.S. Air Force photo
gbu10.scopeNote: A Phantom carrying a GBU-10. Laser-guided Paveways have been in the U.S. inventory since the Vietnam era and are still used on the A-10C.

gbu10.title: Lockheed F-117A Nighthawk 79-10781 GBU-10A Paveway II Cold War NMUSAF 26Sep09 (14413518150)
gbu10.author: Valder137
gbu10.scopeNote: A GBU-10A Paveway II under an F-117 at the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force — the same family of 2,000-pound laser-guided bombs.

litening.title: A-10 Warthog - Litening (Balikatan 2016)
litening.author: RoyKabanlit
litening.scopeNote: An AN/AAQ-28 Litening pod on an A-10 at Balikatan. Litening gives the A-10C a laser designator plus infrared and electro-optical sensors.

litening.title: 130110-f-oc707-000 Female A-10 Thunderbolt II Pilot Maj. Olivia Elliott examines the LITENING advanced targeting pod
litening.author: U.S. Air Force photo / Samuel King Jr.
litening.scopeNote: An A-10 pilot checks the Litening pod before flight. The rounded nose holds the sensors that find and designate targets.

litening.title: ANAAQ-28 LITENING
litening.author: Hunini
litening.scopeNote: AN/AAQ-28 Litening in profile. Litening II reached U.S. forces in 1999 and is the pod carried on this A-10C model.

litening.title: USMC-18198
litening.author: http://www.marines.mil/unit/3rdmaw/PublishingImages/2006/avi2.jpg
litening.scopeNote: Marines pack a Litening pod into its shipping case. The crate is stencilled LITENING — the same targeting system used on the A-10C.

litening.title: A-10 AF80-0258 on final Jagel Air Defender 23
litening.author: Boevaya mashina
litening.scopeNote: An A-10C on final, targeting pod on a starboard wing station — the usual home for Litening on the Thunderbolt II.

litening.title: Litening Pod on FA-18
litening.author: US Govermen
litening.scopeNote: A Litening pod under an F/A-18. The AN/AAQ-28 is used across U.S. types; on the A-10C it designates for laser-guided bombs such as the GBU-10.

litening.title: Northrop+Grumman AN-AAQ 28 LITENING AT mounted on F-16 at NATO Days 2023
litening.author: Boevaya mashina
litening.scopeNote: A Northrop Grumman AN/AAQ-28 Litening AT at close range. The pod’s laser can mark a target for the A-10’s Paveway weapons.

tails.title: A10 chaff and flares
tails.author: The original uploader was EH101 at Italian Wikipedia. U.S. Air Force Photo by Tech. Sgt. Kevin J. Gruenwald
tails.scopeNote: Twin tails from dead astern, with flares already away. The A-10’s vertical stabilizers are interchangeable left and right.

tails.title: Thunderbolts set off flares (14998869902)
tails.author: US Air Force from USA
tails.scopeNote: A pair of A-10s pop flares over a sea of cloud. The twin tails and high engines are the type’s unmistakable rear view.

tails.title: U.S. Air Force A-10 Thunderbolt IIs fire flares 190815-F-ZD147-0088
tails.author: U.S. Department of Defense Current Photos
tails.scopeNote: A-10s fire flares in a trailing formation. Those two fins also shield the engines from some incoming missiles’ view.

tails.title: A-10 serial 79-147 rear view
tails.author: Extrapolaris
tails.scopeNote: Both vertical tails of 79-147 up close on the ramp — the same interchangeable left-and-right design the Air Force still highlights.

tails.title: A-10 Thunderbolt rear at Dubai Airshow 2019
tails.author: Mztourist
tails.scopeNote: Straight on to the empennage at the Dubai Airshow: two tails, two engines, one A-10.

tails.title: A-10 Thunderbolt II drops flares - 081112-F-7823A-484
tails.author: Staff Sgt. Aaron Allmon
tails.scopeNote: Flares drop away behind an A-10. The twin tails stay in the shot — a layout chosen so the jet can keep flying after heavy damage.

tails.title: 422d TES A-10C Flares - Aviation Nation 2019
tails.author: Noah Wulf
tails.scopeNote: An A-10C of the 422nd Test and Evaluation Squadron dumps flares at Aviation Nation. The twin tails bookend the high-mounted TF34s.

decelerons.title: An A-10 Thunderbolt II from Selfridge Air National Guard Base, Michigan, prepares to land on a public highway in Alpena, Michigan, August 5, 2021
decelerons.author: Master Sgt. Scott Thompson
decelerons.scopeNote: Split-aileron ‘decelerons’ wide open as a Selfridge A-10 lands on a public highway. The outboard ailerons open like a clamshell to act as speed brakes.

decelerons.title: A-10 Highway US Michigan
decelerons.author: U.S. Air National Guard photo by Master Sgt. Scott Thompson
decelerons.scopeNote: The same highway strip, this time on short final. The A-10’s unswept straight wing and those big ailerons help it land short and slow.

decelerons.title: US Airmen make history with highway landing 160620-F-IM659-138
decelerons.author: Senior Airman Nicole Keim
decelerons.scopeNote: Touching down on an austere strip, smoke at the mains. The A-10’s straight wing and split ailerons were designed for this kind of landing.

decelerons.title: Sand land 141203-F-NI493-120
decelerons.author: Airman 1st Class Ryan Callaghan
decelerons.scopeNote: An A-10 settles onto a dry lake. Head-on you can read the unswept wing that fills most of the trailing edge with aileron.

decelerons.title: 107th Fighter Squadron conducts austere landings (4466476)
decelerons.author: U.S. Air Force photo by Master Sgt. David Kujawa
decelerons.scopeNote: On approach with the gear down: a clear look at the A-10’s long, straight wing — the platform those split-aileron decelerons are built into.

decelerons.title: 107th Fighter Squadron conducts austere landings (4466470)
decelerons.author: U.S. Air Force photo by Master Sgt. David Kujawa
decelerons.scopeNote: A heritage-painted A-10 of the 107th Fighter Squadron on short final. The straight wing is doing what it was meant to do: fly slowly and still roll.

gear_pods.title: 80-0244 OS an OA-10A of 51 FW 25 FS (3224633529)
gear_pods.author: Jerry Gunner from Lincoln, UK
gear_pods.scopeNote: In flight, gear up: the main-wheel fairing hangs under the wing, and the tyre is still partly visible. That is the A-10’s famous gear pod.

gear_pods.title: An air-to-air left side view of an OA-10 Thunderbolt II aircraft of the 23rd Tactical Air Support Squadron in-flight over the desert Southwest DF-ST-88-07164
gear_pods.author: Tech. Sgt. Michael Haggerty
gear_pods.scopeNote: A classic side-on portrait over the desert. Under each wing the retracted main gear sits in a pod, wheel peeking out — built to survive a gear-up landing.

gear_pods.title: An air-to-air left side view of an OA-10 Thunderbolt II aircraft of the 23rd Tactical Air Support Squadron firing it's GAU-8-A Avenger 30mm cannon at a target on the East Tactical Range in Southern Arizona DF-ST-88-07165
gear_pods.author: Tech. Sgt. Michael Haggerty
gear_pods.scopeNote: Banking over the desert with the mains tucked into their pods. The wheels stay partly exposed even when the gear is up.

gear_pods.title: 80-0244 OS an OA-10A of 51 FW 25 FS (3225488810)
gear_pods.author: Jerry Gunner from Lincoln, UK
gear_pods.scopeNote: Another pass on the same jet: the rounded main-gear pod is visible just forward of the wing stores.

gear_pods.title: 355th Fighter Squadron A-OA-10 Thunderbolt II, Exercise Northern Edge '99 on March 9, 1999
gear_pods.author: Tech. Sgt. David W. Richards, U.S. Air Force
gear_pods.scopeNote: Two A-10s over snow. From this angle the under-wing gear pods — and the partly exposed wheels — are easy to pick out.

gear_pods.title: 184th Fighter Squadron A-10 Flaredrop
gear_pods.author: United States Air Force
gear_pods.scopeNote: From below, a flare already away: the wing pods that house the retracted mains sit mid-span, a hallmark of the A-10 in flight.
